caption: Sampling and the Nyquist limit in the frequency domain, with a worked example at fs = 48 kHz. Sampling copies the signal's spectrum around every multiple of the sample rate. Top panel: a signal band-limited to 20 kHz sampled at 48 kHz - the copies sit far away, so a low-pass filter lifts the original back out. Bottom panel: the band now reaches 30 kHz, past fs/2 = 24 kHz - the copy centered at 48 kHz folds back inside the band, and a 30 kHz tone is heard as an alias at 48 - 30 = 18 kHz. The fix is the anti-alias filter before the sampler: cut everything above fs/2 first, because after sampling an alias can never be filtered out. The same copy-removal logic sits after a DAC - its output low-pass filter removes the spurious sampling artifacts (pool E8A10) - and flash converters serve SDRs because their very high speed digitizes high frequencies (E8A08).
spoken: Two spectrum panels share one frequency axis, drawn for a 48 kilohertz sample rate. In the top panel the signal is band-limited to 20 kHz. Its spectrum is a smooth bump near zero, and faint dashed copies of that bump sit centered on 48 and 96 kHz, far from the original - nothing overlaps, so a low-pass filter can recover the signal cleanly. A solid line marks fs over 2, 24 kHz, the Nyquist limit. In the bottom panel the band reaches 30 kHz, past that limit. Now the dashed copy centered on 48 kHz reaches back across 24 kHz and lands inside the band - the overlap is shaded. A tone at 30 kHz folds back around the Nyquist line and is heard at 48 minus 30, 18 kHz: an alias that was never really there, and that no filter can remove afterward. The fix is drawn as a dashed low-pass shape, the anti-alias filter before the sampler: cut everything above half the sample rate first. The same idea in reverse is the pool's DAC output filter, which removes the spurious sampling copies.
